name: Boat speed
seoDesc: Boat speed: work out shaft horsepower (P) from the boat displacement and the crouch's constant. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units…
summary: shaft horsepower (P) is what the Boat speed calculator works out, and it gets there from the boat displacement, the crouch's constant and the speed. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Boat speed calculator work?
sections.html:
The Boat speed calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports shaft horsepower (P) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the boat displacement (D), the crouch's constant (C) and the speed (S).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilometers per hour. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Boat speed calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Shaft horsepower (P)=boat displacement (D) × (speed (S) ^ 2) ÷ (crouch's constant (C) ^ 2)
Boat type=crouch's constant (C)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Boat type set to Cruisers. Straight away the calculator returns Crouch's constant (C) = 150.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Crouch's constant (C) = 150 should be roughly the size you expected from Boat type set to Cruisers.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in kilowatts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Boat speed calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the boat displacement, the crouch's constant and the speed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Boat speed calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns shaft horsepower (P), derived from the boat displacement, the crouch's constant and the speed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Boat speed calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the boat displacement, the crouch's constant and the speed, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter shaft horsepower (P) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Shaft horsepower (P) opens in kilowatts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Crouch's constant (C) = 150. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Boat speed calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
